# Dose-Response Modelling of Sodium Chloride on Seed Germination

## Abstract
Seed germination of table salt (NaCl) treated samples was measured at 20 °C, and the germination rate decreased from 92.4 % to 61.8 % as the concentration increased from 0 mM to 150 mM. The half-maximal inhibitory concentration was 74.6 mM (Table 1), and the fitted coefficient was r = -0.93 (p < 0.01) [1]. These results suggest that NaCl may delay water uptake rather than damage the embryo [2].

## 2 Methods
Seeds were incubated on filter paper moistened with 5 mL of solution for 7 days, and the germination rate was recorded every 24 h (Fig. 1).

Table 1. Fitted dose-response parameters (mean ± sd, n = 3).
Concentration (mM)	Germination (%)	Rate (day^-1)
0	92.4	1.71
150	61.8	0.98

## 3 Results
The relationship between concentration and germination was not linear across the whole range, so we used the following empirical model:

G = G0 / (1 + C / IC50)    (1)

where G is the germination rate and C is the concentration. Germination did not recover after the salt was removed, which indicates an osmotic rather than a toxic effect.

Fig. 1. Germination rate (%) versus concentration (mM); error bars show ± sd (n = 3).

## References
[1] Almeida RP, Costa LS. Osmotic stress and seed vigour. Journal of Seed Science, 2019.
[2] Chen H, et al. Ion toxicity in germinating seeds. Plant Physiology Reports, 2021.
